title: Multiply with a curried first argument
security_scope: Canonical tutorial module returning data, not a coin puzzle or an authorization policy. The original multiplies two unbounded signed CLVM integers read by position and is curried on the page into a doubler; this port multiplies two canonical signed 64-bit integers through the strict typed ABI. Declared per-case divergences record where the original's unbounded and untyped environment reading differs. Each build's standard curried instance is constructed separately and executed in all five builds; the Chialisp build's instance is compared with the page's spelled curried result. Finite differential tests are not a compiler-correctness proof, and a curried instance hash commits a coin to a program without making it safe.

source_adaptation.description: Copy the complete fenced module source lines exactly, including their comments and original LF endings.

limitations: Rust i64 arithmetic is finite and checked; the original CLVM integers are unbounded. Overflow rejects in Rust where the original returns a larger result.
The default strict Rust ABI rejects padded, noncanonical and out-of-range integer atoms, extra list elements and improper tails that the original module ignores or reads as integers.
Every such difference is declared per case and checked against independently specified CLVM bytes; declared divergences never cover Rust CLVM, which must match the native Rust source.
The original module is compiled unchanged; no argument guard or wrapper is added. Behavioral comparison does not require equal CLVM bytes or tree hashes.

Curried instances use the standard form (a (q . M) (c (q . A) 1)) built independently with clvmr and cross-checked against the SDK's owned constructor and hash arithmetic. Only the Chialisp build's instance is compared with the page's curried result; the Rust instances are different programs with different hashes, and no identity is claimed for the Rue instances even where their bytes coincide.

Curried instance cases carry no declared divergences, so they only use inputs on which every build agrees. The SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE naming variant is a convention, not a separate program, and is not ported.

cases.label: tutorial values: the page doubler applied to five
page reuse values: five times five
overflow rejects in Rust; the original grows

declared_divergence.reason: Checked i64 multiplication overflows and rejects; the original returns the unbounded product.

cases.label: negating the minimum rejects in Rust; the original grows

declared_divergence.reason: Checked i64 multiplication overflows at the minimum and rejects; the original returns the unbounded product.

cases.label: value above i64 rejects in Rust

declared_divergence.reason: The original accepts unbounded integers; the typed Rust i64 ABI rejects values outside its 64-bit range.

cases.label: padded atom rejects in Rust; the original reads it as two

declared_divergence.reason: The original reads any atom as a signed integer, so a padded encoding is accepted; the typed Rust ABI rejects noncanonical integer atoms.

cases.label: explicit zero byte rejects in Rust; the original reads it as zero

declared_divergence.reason: The original reads 0x00 as the integer 0; the typed Rust ABI only accepts the empty atom for zero.

cases.label: extra argument ignored by the original

declared_divergence.reason: The original reads arguments by position and ignores trailing environment values; the typed Rust ABI rejects extra list elements.

cases.label: improper tail ignored by the original

declared_divergence.reason: The original reads arguments by position and ignores an improper tail; the typed Rust ABI requires a proper argument list.
